title: Memory and Undefined Behavior
description: Undefined, implementation-defined, and unspecified behavior, and the memory-safety bugs that stem from them.
objectives: Distinguish undefined, implementation-defined, and unspecified behavior
Recognize the major categories of memory-safety bugs in C
Understand why relying on undefined behavior is dangerous even when it 'seems to work'

content.heading: Three Kinds of 'It Depends'
content.body: The C standard distinguishes three categories of behavior it doesn't fully pin down. Undefined behavior (UB) means the standard places absolutely no requirements on what happens — the program might crash, produce nonsensical output, appear to work correctly, or (in principle) do literally anything; compilers are explicitly permitted to assume UB never occurs and optimize accordingly, which can make code relying on it behave differently (or 'break') under a different compiler, optimization level, or even an unrelated code change elsewhere in the same file. Implementation-defined behavior means the standard requires each specific compiler/platform to choose a defined, documented behavior, but different implementations are allowed to choose differently (e.g., the exact size of int, or whether >> on a negative number sign-extends). Unspecified behavior is similar but doesn't require the implementation to document its choice at all (e.g., the order function arguments are evaluated in).

content.heading: Common Memory-Safety Bugs, All Undefined Behavior
content.body:
Buffer overflow: writing past the end of an allocated block (an array or malloc'd buffer), corrupting adjacent memory. Invalid pointer use: dereferencing a NULL, wild (uninitialized), or dangling (already-freed) pointer. Uninitialized variables: reading a local variable's value before it's been assigned anything meaningful. Out-of-bounds access: reading or writing an array index outside its valid range — C performs no bounds checking, so this compiles and often 'runs', just incorrectly and unpredictably. Strict aliasing: a more subtle rule stating that accessing memory through a pointer of an incompatible type (e.g., reinterpreting a float* as an int* without a union) is technically UB, even though it might seem to work, since it can confuse compiler optimizations that assume pointers of different types don't refer to overlapping memory. Lifetime issues: using an object (like a local variable, or freed heap memory) after its lifetime has ended.

The danger of UB specifically is that 'it happened to work when I tested it' is not evidence of correctness — a program invoking UB has no defined behavior at all, and can fail unpredictably later, on a different machine, compiler version, or optimization setting, precisely because the compiler was never obligated to make it behave consistently in the first place.

content.explanation: Each commented line compiles just fine — the compiler is not required to detect or reject undefined behavior. Their actual runtime effect is entirely unspecified by the C standard, which is exactly what makes UB dangerous to rely on, even 'accidentally', without noticing.

keyPoints: Undefined behavior means the standard gives NO guarantees — anything can happen, including 'seeming to work'
Implementation-defined behavior is pinned down per-platform/compiler but can differ between them
Buffer overflows, invalid pointer dereferences, uninitialized reads, and out-of-bounds access are all UB
Code that 'happens to work' while invoking UB is not proven correct — it can break under a different compiler or setting
commonMistakes: Treating 'it worked when I ran it' as proof that code invoking undefined behavior is actually correct
Assuming the compiler will catch out-of-bounds access, uninitialized reads, or invalid pointer use (it generally won't)
Reinterpreting a pointer's type casually, unaware of C's strict aliasing rule
